item.title: Meet the Woman Who Stands to Inherit Much of Jeffrey Epstein’s Fortune
item.description:
The young dentist was smiling and soft-spoken, wearing a Columbia University fleece jacket and holding her long hair back with a clip. She was introduced by her assistant simply as “Dr. Karyna.”

But what the patient — who had come to the office in December expecting to see a different dentist — didn’t know was that she was being treated by Dr. Karyna Shuliak, the notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s girlfriend.

Dr. Shuliak was the last person Mr. Epstein called before he killed himself in his jail cell in 2019. She could inherit as much as $100 million from his estate, including a 33-carat diamond ring, according to a trove of investigative records released by federal authorities.

But on that winter day, Dr. Shuliak was working as a part-time dentist in an unremarkable office in Downtown Brooklyn, according to dentists who work or used to work at the practice.

Her attempt to forge something of a normal life, though, was soon shattered when the Justice Department released three million pages of investigative files and emails it had gathered on Mr. Epstein. The files, released in late January, included thousands of intimate emails between Dr. Shuliak and Mr. Epstein and dozens of photographs of her and of them together.

Suddenly, their nearly eight-year relationship was on vivid display for all to see. They had fights about sex — with both wanting more at different times. She placed orders to a sexual wellness company for couples. She periodically sent him links to graphic pornographic videos. In some emails they discussed birth control pills and acne medications and treatments.

Dr. Shuliak, 37, emerges as a complicated and unusual figure in Mr. Epstein’s world, based on a close review of the files and conversations with several people familiar with her. A native of Belarus who met Mr. Epstein when she was 21, she has not identified herself as a victim, nor have federal authorities considered her a co-conspirator in Mr. Epstein’s sex trafficking. There is no indication that the Federal Bureau of Investigation ever interviewed her, and lawyers for hundreds of his victims have never deposed her.

He once called her his “favorite” and often told her he loved her. She had free use of a credit card to buy whatever she wanted. They jetted around the world together, and he funneled payments of nearly $1 million to her over the years. He also sent tens of thousands of dollars to her parents in Belarus, the files reveal.

Over the years, she earned enough of his trust to help manage his properties and staff and even played a critical role in his effort to buy a Moroccan palace just weeks before his 2019 arrest.

Mr. Epstein controlled the relationship, but there is little doubt she benefited from it professionally, personally and financially.

The emails reveal new details about how Mr. Epstein helped her get into Columbia University’s dental school — and how he helped her obtain U.S. citizenship by asking one of his female victims to marry her.

In one email he suggested that the fastest “way to a green card” was through a same-sex marriage.

This year, congressional Democrats accused Mr. Epstein of exploiting the immigration system and called out Dr. Shuliak’s marriage to an American woman, which ended in divorce, as a potentially “illusory” one. U.S. immigration authorities have not challenged the process through which Dr. Shuliak obtained her citizenship.

As of this spring, Dr. Shuliak had been living in the Upper East Side condo building in which Mr. Epstein’s brother, Mark, has a financial stake.

Through her lawyer, she declined to comment.

In a brief interview, Mark Epstein said, “I only wish that woman the best.”

A friend of Dr. Shuliak’s from Belarus, who once shared an apartment with her in Brooklyn and asked not be named to protect her privacy, said she believed Dr. Shuliak “truly loved” Jeffrey Epstein.

Karyna Shuliak had lived in New York for only nine months when she met Mr. Epstein in late March 2011.

She had moved from Belarus on a temporary student visa to study English at a school in Manhattan. She was making about $15 an hour as a dental assistant and applying for waitressing jobs while she tried to figure out how to continue the dental education she had begun in Belarus.

A young woman from Siberia would introduce her to Mr. Epstein, the files show. The woman said in an interview with The New York Times that she had periodically been expected to recruit other young women, presumably to provide Mr. Epstein with sexualized massages. And that appeared to be Mr. Epstein’s intention with Dr. Shuliak.

The woman, who asked not to be named because she said Mr. Epstein had abused her, had sent Mr. Epstein a photo of Dr. Shuliak, describing her as pretty. After some back and forth, it was decided that the woman, Dr. Shuliak and her roommate from Belarus would meet Mr. Epstein at his Manhattan mansion.

“Go slow,” the woman advised Mr. Epstein in an email.

Their first encounters fit the familiar pattern he used with other women. Mr. Epstein flattered, pampered and tried to manipulate her, the files show. Almost immediately, he offered to help her realize her dream of becoming a dentist.

But the emails show that Dr. Shuliak pushed back — at least in the first few months.

A few weeks after they met, she wrote to Mr. Epstein, telling him she thought he was a “remarkable person.” But she added that she could not accept his help “due to some views which strongly stay in my mind, no matter how stupid it may look.”

“I wish you all the best and apologize if I wasted your time,” she added.

Though she doesn’t specify what upset her, their introduction occurred after Mr. Epstein had pleaded guilty in Florida to a charge of soliciting prostitution from an underage teenager and had been accused of abusing dozens of other teenagers.

His response was to berate her for listening to “rumors and stories.”

She responded: “This world is very cruel sometimes and in most cases we have to pay a certain price for things. I should say that I have read some information about you.”

Mr. Epstein, who was 58 at the time, did not take no for an answer. The emails released by federal prosecutors show that he bought Dr. Shuliak and her roommate tickets to see “The Lion King” on Broadway and dinners at restaurants. He treated her to a scenic helicopter ride around Manhattan. By July 2011, she had visited his New Mexico ranch; a few months later, his private island residence in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Ever since she was a child, Dr. Shuliak wanted to be a dentist.

She was inspired by her own family’s dental problems and what she saw as the poor dental health in Belarus, she wrote in an admissions essay to dental school reviewed by The Times. She had completed four of five years of dental school in Minsk, but stopped her studies to go to New York.

By the winter of 2012, she accepted Mr. Epstein’s help to get into dental school. After Columbia’s College of Dental Medicine initially rejected her, Mr. Epstein asked his own dentist, Dr. Thomas J. Magnani, a powerful alumnus, to put him in contact with the dental school dean. Mr. Epstein dangled the idea of making up to a $10 million donation. In the end, he would give only about $210,000 to Columbia, according to an accounting by the university, but it was enough to grease the wheels.

The Justice Department files include a text message chain showing how Dr. Magnani and Dr. James Fine, a dental school administrator, gave Dr. Shuliak a heads-up on the topics she would encounter during an admissions exam in April 2012 to test her practical skills as a transfer student. Neither Dr. Magnani nor Dr. Fine responded to a request for comment.

After she passed and Columbia admitted her, Mr. Epstein arranged for Dr. Shuliak’s mother to visit from Belarus. He would pay her tuition for her three years of school.

“You are the purest man out of all men,” Dr. Shuliak wrote to him in June 2012.

“All your love and care, my parents, school, apartment. THANK YOU SOOO MUCH FOR EVERYTHING!!!”

They fought at times over his insistence on having sex with other women in their 20s, including with the small group of assistants who did chores for him and whom he referred to as his “family,” according to the emails.

“I understand you need it, however these are the things that don’t feel natural to me, it feels somewhat dirty to me,” she wrote to him in August 2012.

Nowhere in the Justice Department files that were reviewed by The Times does Dr. Shuliak express a broader ethical concern about how he was treating those other women, many of whom would later claim to be victims of his abuse. Instead, she asked Mr. Epstein to keep his relations with those women out of her sight.

“If that is not a lot to ask, please enjoy it but keep me away from it,” she wrote. “I will stay with you no matter what, as long as you are happy. I love you.”

By the time she applied to Columbia in 2012, Dr. Shuliak had overstayed the student visa she obtained in 2010.

In early 2013, Mr. Epstein found a solution to keep her in the country, the files show. Two years earlier, New York became one of the first states to legalize same-sex marriage. Mr. Epstein concluded that a marriage in New York between two women might be the easiest way to gain U.S. citizenship without raising red flags that the marriage was arranged solely to avoid deportation.

Mr. Epstein chose, from the ranks of his assistants, a 30-year-old woman from Minnesota to be her spouse.

Brad Edwards, the lawyer for the woman, said that his client was a victim of Mr. Epstein and that he could not speak about her situation. But he said that, as a general rule, “nobody was permitted or dared ever to disobey Jeffrey Epstein.”

The emails show that Mr. Epstein instructed the woman to meet Dr. Shuliak on the morning of Sept. 16, 2013, at the New York City Marriage Bureau. She was told to have her bags packed so she could immediately fly to the Virgin Islands after getting the marriage license, while Dr. Shuliak would stay behind to attend her dental school classes.

The women were married three weeks later at the Office of the City Clerk. Photos were taken of the ceremony.

After the wedding, a Brooklyn immigration lawyer working for Mr. Epstein submitted an immigration form stating that the woman wanted to list Dr. Shuliak as her wife and beneficiary. The request was approved, and immigration officials dismissed Dr. Shuliak’s pending deportation proceedings.

Months after the marriage, Dr. Shuliak got a green card, making her a lawful resident.

Outwardly, the marriage had signs of legitimacy. The two women shared an apartment in the Upper East Side building that was partly owned by Mr. Epstein’s brother and where Mr. Epstein had housed many of his assistants. They had a joint bank account at Deutsche Bank and went on trips together to London, Europe and Japan.

In May 2018, she officially became a U.S. citizen. A year later Dr. Shuliak and her spouse divorced. According to a report released this year by Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, Dr. Shuliak’s former wife claimed she had been forced into marriage. The woman, in a statement to the Epstein estate, said she had not known that the wedding had been scheduled just days before Dr. Shuliak’s deportation hearing.

The report concluded that the marriage may have been done to provide Dr. Shuliak with the “legal basis to continue residing in the United States.” It did not recommend any legal challenge to her citizenship.

In early 2019, Dr. Shuliak and Mr. Epstein seemed every bit a couple. She was living most of the time in his New York mansion and took along her cat, Blueberry, when they traveled together.

She had become a licensed dentist in the U.S. Virgin Islands, Florida and New Mexico after completing dental school in 2015. But there is no evidence that she had much of a practice, even though the files detail dental equipment installed at some of his residences. Instead, she spent much of her energy helping to manage his properties and staff.

No task seemed too small. She instructed his drivers to keep “cold Voss water” in Mr. Epstein’s cars, organized a floral installation for his Manhattan mansion, ordered a shipping container filled with outdoor furniture for his island and managed repairs and cleaning schedules for the Upper East Side apartments that his brother was invested in.

In mid-June 2019, the pair traveled together to Paris, where Mr. Epstein had an apartment. On July 6, Mr. Epstein returned home to the United States, while Dr. Shuliak remained in Europe. When his plane touched down at Teterboro Airport in New Jersey, federal agents were waiting and arrested him.

About a month after his arrest, in a 20-minute phone call from a jail in Lower Manhattan, Mr. Epstein told Dr. Shuliak that the federal sex-trafficking charges would take longer to resolve than he had thought. He advised her to find another place to stay for the time being, according to an account of the call provided by her lawyer to federal authorities. The lawyer, Maurice Sercarz, said he had told her “to be strong.”

The next morning, Aug. 10, 2019, Mr. Epstein was found to have died by suicide in his jail cell.

Shortly before his death, Mr. Epstein amended his will to leave to her much of the $600 million fortune he had at the time, including the large diamond ring “in contemplation of marriage,” according to a handwritten note on a related document. But how much she will actually receive is unclear. The estate is worth between $120 million and $200 million after paying out large sums to his victims, records show. There are dozens of beneficiaries in addition to Dr. Shuliak, including Mark Epstein’s children, who stand to inherit $10 million.

Yet despite this potential windfall, Dr. Shuliak did not give up on her desire to be a dentist. By 2023, she was back in New York applying for a postdoctoral dental program at Columbia, apparently to fulfill a requirement she needed to obtain a license to practice in the state.

The same two dentists who helped her gain admission to Columbia in 2012 once again came to her assistance, according to a copy of her admissions file reviewed by The Times. The file shows that Dr. Fine, the dean overseeing Columbia’s postgraduate residency programs, created a special “faculty internship” for her at the Midtown Manhattan dental practice he shared with Dr. Magnani.

Both men gave her their highest recommendation for the program, which she graduated from in May 2025 along with six other students. In November, she received her dental license to practice in New York.

In the aftermath of the release of the Epstein files, Columbia demoted Dr. Fine and removed Dr. Magnani from his alumni leadership posts. The men declined to comment. The university did not recommend any consequences for Dr. Shuliak, who it said had met the qualifications for admission.

At around the same time as she received her New York dental license, Dr. Shuliak answered a want ad on Indeed.com for a part-time job as a dentist in Downtown Brooklyn, according to a dentist with the practice, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss workplace issues. It was there that Yoonhae Kim, a patient, was treated by her twice, for a cleaning in December and a filling in February.

Ms. Kim said she hadn’t realized Dr. Shuliak’s true identity until she saw photographs of her released with the Epstein files. Feeling duped because she was not informed of Dr. Shuliak’s full name and wanting to warn other patients, she reached out to The Times.

“I was so upset,” Ms. Kim said. “I just couldn’t believe it. Of all the things that happened to me, I didn’t win the lottery. I met Epstein’s girlfriend.”

Dr. Shuliak’s last day working at the Brooklyn office was Feb. 12. She was supposed to work on Feb. 16, but she called in sick and never returned. The notoriety from the files probably made it difficult for her to keep working there, the dentist at the practice said. Dr. Shuliak’s lawyer declined to say whether she had gotten another dental job.

Kitty Bennett and Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: A Different Kind of Grocery Store Magnate
item.description:
On a rainy March morning, 25 folding chairs were set out on the floor of Meadow Lane, a gourmet market in Lower Manhattan that is normally brimming with influencers, Tribeca moms and finance bros picking up lunch. Today the place belonged to McKinsey & Company.

The consultants are the ones who had requested the meeting. They wanted to know just how Meadow Lane had become such a thriving business in such a short time. They shook out their umbrellas and found their seats among the artisanal crackers, sea-moss beverages and carefully arranged jars of honey.

Sammy Nussdorf, the store’s 29-year-old owner, watched them settle in. Then he began to talk.

He told the consultants about the long permit purgatory he had endured before opening for business. He told them about the $65 olive oil and the $12 chicken salad. He told them about the kitchen’s struggles to keep up with demand. He even told them about the undercooked chicken nuggets that, much to his horror, became international news. By the time he was done, the consultants had questions.

Why stock Mexican Coke?

Nussdorf said he wanted an eclectic mix, rather than the usual health mart monoculture.

How did he select the brands for his shelves?

He had spent a year taste-testing products before opening, he said. And he made space for new products by not charging emerging indie brands a so-called slotting fee, unlike so many other retailers.

Did social media help?

Oh, yes. In fact, he considered his TikTok followers to be something like partners in the enterprise.

Satisfied, the consultants filled bags with products and snacks before thanking him for his time and heading back into the rain.

On the morning of the confab, Meadow Lane had been open 90 days. In that time, Nussdorf said, the store had served 80,000 customers while generating $3 million in revenue. On a given day, he said, more than 1,000 people passed through the 2,000-square-foot space on Greenwich Street.

“Operating a business like this in a place like New York is a nightmare,” he said. “I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone. But it’s so good.”

He grew up on the Upper East Side, right across Fifth Avenue from the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He is the youngest son of Glenn Nussdorf, the chief executive of a family business, Quality King Distributors, a multibillion-dollar distributor of health and beauty products and prescription drugs.

Forbes has ranked the Nussdorfs among the 150 richest families in America. Sammy’s father, who keeps a low public profile, has asked to be removed from the listing.

“My family and I, we never talked about money,” Sammy said. “We’ve never discussed inheritance, assets, values, anything. I have no idea. I can guesstimate, if I wanted to, but I don’t really care.”

Nussdorf was cutting stems and arranging flowers (Japanese sweet peas and allium) in the studio off the main floor of Meadow Lane as he spoke of finding his way. He struggled academically during his years at Columbia Grammar and Prep, a private school on the Upper West Side. By his own account, he was a party kid, staying out in the clubs till 5 a.m. on school nights when he was 14.

He started a food Instagram in high school, documenting the Bolognese sauce and aglio e olio he made from scratch. As a sociology major at New York University, he hosted dinner parties in his first apartment.

Three blocks from where he lived, his father had a family investment office, Spring St. Group, and Sammy started working there in the summers. By the time he graduated in 2019, he was well versed in venture capital. Soon enough he assumed leadership duties.

“Nepotism awarded me the privilege to be in that position,” he said. “But the money that opened Meadow Lane is money I made in V.C.” He took a pause. “A lot of people didn’t believe it.”

While toiling in finance, he got serious about a hobby — floral arrangements. He would wake at 5 a.m. to source flowers at the markets along West 28th Street and deliver them to friends. He was drifting back to a version of himself crowded out by spreadsheets. He started envisioning a flower-and-coffee shop. He would call it Meadow Lane, after the five-mile strip in Southampton widely known as Billionaires Row, where the Nussdorf family has a home.

He scored a job with Jeff Leatham, a Los Angeles florist whose client list reads like a seating chart at the Met Gala. Friends from the East Coast would FaceTime Nussdorf to find him in a basement snipping stems. Away from the orchids and peonies, he found himself in the aisles of Erewhon, a high-end organic grocery store that was fast becoming an influencers’ hangout.

Ready to act on his plan, he returned to New York. But he quickly realized his original notion of a store devoted to flowers and coffee wasn’t going to cut it. There would have to be prepared foods, Peruvian grapes, matcha powder.

After signing a lease, he commissioned marketing agency proposals, only to find that the pros offered “really boring things for $15,000 a month,” he said. So he started a TikTok account.

The first thing he needed was a catchy handle. “Something really cringe,” he said. He decided on Brokeback Contessa, a melding of “Brokeback Mountain” and Ina Garten’s “Barefoot Contessa.” In an early video, Nussdorf explained that he was going to build a grocery store and document the process, start to finish, warts and all.

He showed himself having a tense meeting with a contractor and then riding an elevator, sunglasses on. A woman asks him to describe the meeting in three words. “Unhinged, disappointing and expensive,” he says. A TikTok star, or at least a viable social-media character, was born.

What happened next was either a master class in modern marketing or the kind of thing that happens when someone with lots of passion and no filter builds something in public. As Nussdorf posted videos detailing his setbacks and moments of doubt, the number of his TikTok followers swelled to more than 150,000.

“I think the more disclosure, the more unveiling of the curtain behind a private business, the more interested people are,” he said.

As Meadow Lane neared its opening date last November, thousands of people were invested in whether the New York City Department of Buildings would approve its gas line. Vogue and Vanity Fair sent reporters and photographers. Soon fans were stopping Nussdorf on the street: Hey, Brokeback! When are we getting the turkey pinwheels?

While building his business, Nussdorf has been managing an addiction.

“I was launching Meadow Lane in and out of rehab,” he said. “That had nothing to do with the delays. It was tough. After work, I would go home and lose control. No sleep. Just trying to fit in my addiction. Trying to hide it, too. It’s a nightmare.”

He said he knew his use of ketamine had gotten out of control. “I was sick of living that way, beholden to a substance that perpetuated isolation and deep sadness,” he said. “My addiction severed me from myself, everyone and everything I love. The journey forward is not easy. It’s a daily decision and practice.”

Meadow Lane helped him through it.

“When you’re in early recovery, you need purpose,” he said. “You need passion. You need a reason to wake up in the morning. It’s great therapy for me, whether I’m behind the table making flowers, which is my meditative state, or I’m helping customers.”

“In a way, I feel like this saved me,” he added. “Meadow Lane and my dog, Schnitzel.” (Schnitzel, for the record, is a mini goldendoodle).

TikTok-driven lines greeted the store’s opening. The kitchen, built for 300 transactions a day, was overwhelmed. At the same time, an online backlash targeted him for selling such high-priced goods. “People are threatening to burn down the store and throw rocks through the windows,” Nussdorf told The New York Post, which had made him a running character.

On day three, videos pinged across social media showing the undercooked chicken nuggets. Nussdorf was certain the mistake would sink him. He tracked down the affected customers and refunded them privately, he said, and he posted a video in which he took responsibility.

“The next day,” he said, “I didn’t think people were coming back — but the lines were longer.”

In the midst of the opening week drama, the celebrity chef Bobby Flay, a neighborhood resident, checked out the store. “He probably had the biggest pre-press in the history of opening a food business,” Flay said in an interview. “We were all paying attention to it.” He approached the owner, who seemed a bit down.

“This is so hard,” Nussdorf told him, Flay recalled.

Flay told him what every restaurateur eventually learns: “You asked for this and you got it. Now comes the practical part. Keep your head down and put out the best food you can every day.”

The pep talk worked.

“He talked me off the cliff,” Nussdorf said. “My entire team was telling me the same thing. But I couldn’t listen to them, because they weren’t Bobby Flay.”

The chaos of the early days is now behind him. Meadow Lane is an oasis of honey-toned wood and mellow lighting. The artichokes and radicchio heads look like components of a gallery installation.

The store’s logic reveals itself slowly, if at all. Heinz ketchup sits near Flamingo Estate olive oil. Duke’s mayonnaise is a few feet from Ballerina Farms protein powder.

“In the beginning, people were upset that we sold Duke’s,” Nussdorf said. “I’m like, it’s just the best mayonnaise! Just because something is on every shelf in America doesn’t mean it’s a bad product.”

He feels the criticism he has received for the prices isn’t warranted, adding that the average prepared meal costs about $22. “My Chipotle order of double protein is more than that,” he said. “Why is everyone so mad at me?”

Frances Trousdale, Nussdorf’s head of operations (and the daughter of Mary Margaret Trousdale, who runs hospitality for Ralph Lauren), has stuck with Nussdorf through the chicken nugget incident and the rehab stints. “We’ve seen it all together,” she said.

She has also seen a business owner who goes by instinct. “Brands, marketing — all of it has gotten so advanced,” Truesdale said. “There’s such exhaustion from that. He missteps. He says the wrong thing. He posts the wrong thing. And I think that, in an age where it’s easier than ever to appear perfect, Sammy is evolving beyond that.”

Asked what he saw himself doing at 50, Nussdorf said he had no idea. More Meadow Lane locations? Maybe. Maybe not. “I should probably make more friends,” he said. “I don’t do much outside of working.”

He clipped another stem and placed the flower in the vase. He held up the finished arrangement for Trousdale to see.

“I love it, Sammy,” she said.

“Yeah,” he said. “I’ve got to do flowers more often.”

item.title: Why Paramount Paused Its Blockbuster $111 Billion Deal for Warner Bros.
item.description:
On a call around 9 p.m. on Thursday, Jeffrey Kessler, the top trial lawyer for the media behemoth Paramount, made a stunning proposal that could stall the company’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery well into next year.

Paramount, which is run by the tech scion David Ellison, was staring down a lengthy legal battle with state attorneys general, who in mid-July had sued to stop the blockbuster merger over antitrust concerns. Both sides seemed poised to spend weeks arguing about in-the-weeds legal motions and scheduling questions that precede a trial.

Then Mr. Kessler, the co-executive chairman of the law firm Winston Taylor, whom Paramount retained for the deal, called the states. Let’s forgo those early legal battles and move to a trial, he suggested, according to three people familiar with the call. Paramount would agree to halt its merger until June at the latest, while the court case played out, clearing the way for a legal showdown that could redefine Hollywood.

Mr. Kessler proposed the delay because Paramount thought going to a trial was the fastest way to complete the deal, according to two people familiar with the matter. At the same time, the company had already faced a series of early setbacks in the states’ lawsuit, including two court-imposed temporary pauses on the acquisition.

“On some level, the parties saw the handwriting on the wall,” said Eric Talley, a professor at Columbia Law School who specializes in corporate law and governance. “Rather than trying to fight it out right now, they waved a very, very small white flag to say, ‘OK, we’re going to delay this on our own accord.’”

The impending courtroom face-off is likely to be one of the most closely watched Hollywood trials in years, involving high-profile figures like Mr. Ellison and his father, the Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who is backing his bid for Warner Bros. Opposition to the deal has mounted in the entertainment industry: The Writers Guild of America has challenged it on the grounds that it will hurt screenwriters.

The delay means that some of America’s most important news and entertainment organizations are trapped in limbo. The fate of CNN, which is owned by Warner Bros., is uncertain. Likewise for HBO, a linchpin of the Warner Bros. streaming business. The ultimate destiny of the Warner Bros. film studio, and its trove of iconic movies, is still up in the air.

The lawsuit from the states is one of the final hurdles to the deal, after the Justice Department declined to challenge the acquisition last month. The states argue that allowing Paramount to merge with Warner Bros. would give the combined company too much power over films released in theaters and, in particular, the blockbusters that account for a large portion of studio revenues. Paramount says that the states are ignoring the dominance of streamers like YouTube and Netflix, viewing the industry through a narrow lens.

Paramount and the states both declared victory after they agreed to the delay. In a statement, Paramount said the pause was “a significant win” because it set up “a direct path to a trial.”

Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, called it “great news,” adding that the states were “eager to continue to make our case.” A spokesman for Warner Bros. Discovery had no comment.

Paramount’s proposal changes its position from just two weeks earlier. On July 13, the state attorneys general requested a voluntary stop on the deal while the litigation played out. Paramount wasn’t willing to freeze past September.

The states went to court for a short pause and won, with Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California saying that the states had made “a strong showing” that the deal would hurt competition.

The company then faced a fight to convince Judge Martínez-Olguín that she should not pause the deal indefinitely while she considered the lawsuit, a so-called preliminary injunction. Paramount asked for an extensive hearing in mid- to late August to make its case against the injunction, and pressed repeatedly for the chance to bring witnesses to that hearing.

That timeline, the states had said in a July 15 filing, was “rushed” and “patently unfair,” because it did not give their lawyers much time to discover new evidence. Instead, the states said a full airing of the evidence — complete with witnesses on the stand — was best saved for a later, full-blown trial.

On Monday, Judge Martínez-Olguín scheduled a hearing on the injunction for Aug. 3, earlier than Paramount wanted, and did not say whether she would allow testimony from witnesses.

On Thursday, Judge Martínez-Olguín asked Paramount, the states and the Writers Guild to meet to try to determine a schedule for arguments over the injunction. She asked them to return with an update the next day, and gave no hint of whether she was likely to give Paramount the hearing it requested.

Hours later, on the call with the states and the Writers Guild, Mr. Kessler proposed the pause that would allow the case to go to trial.

Bill Kovacic, a former Republican chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, said that if the judge had put an indefinite pause on the deal, it could have created the perception of “further setbacks” for the merger. Instead, by moving right to a trial, the company will be able to marshal its most persuasive case.

“One explanation is that they want more time to formulate the case, to tell the story as completely and favorably as they can,” he said, adding that the states will also be able to use the time to build out their arguments.

Paramount’s willingness to wait until the deal’s expiration in June was meant to signal to Judge Martínez-Olguín that the company was trying to be constructive, two people familiar with the case said. But Paramount will still look to move as quickly as possible within the court’s guidance.

A prolonged delay will be costly for Paramount. To get its deal approved, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders $650 million for every quarter the deal doesn’t close, beginning in October. And if regulators blow up the deal, Paramount owes Warner Bros. Discovery a $7 billion breakup fee.

So far, Warner Bros. has largely deferred to Paramount’s approach to the legal battle with the states, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Hashing out a trial date will be the next twist in the legal saga. In the flurry of negotiations on Thursday and Friday, Paramount and the states agreed to submit their proposed trial schedules next Friday. But they appear to be far apart on that point: Paramount is targeting a November court date, and the states have said they want to go to trial sometime next year, two people familiar with the matter said.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Meta’s Giant Data Center in Louisiana
item.description:
Along the Mississippi Delta in the northeast corner of Louisiana, Meta is building one of the largest artificial intelligence data centers in the world. The tech giant’s project will cost $50 billion and cover roughly six square miles.

Behind the scenes, an extraordinary amount of secrecy was necessary to pull it off. Energy company executives, Louisiana’s governor, state and local officials and representatives of Meta worked on the deal over nine months before it was made public. The project’s speed and covertness have been trumpeted as a model for the entire tech industry.

To report on the project, New York Times reporters interviewed more than 40 people in Richland Parish, Baton Rouge, New Orleans, New York and Silicon Valley, and examined corporate filings, tax records, property records and meeting transcripts.

Here are five takeaways from our reporting:

When Meta’s employees scouted Louisiana and nearby states for potential data center sites, it was Louisiana’s largest energy company, and not state officials, that first pitched the Silicon Valley company on Richland Parish.

Phillip May, Entergy Louisiana’s chief executive, was involved in every step of the process, from securing a tax rebate on data center equipment to buying nearby land and drafting nondisclosure agreements for government officials. The energy company’s promise to build dedicated natural gas turbines for Meta — enough to power the city of New Orleans seven times over — is what separated Louisiana’s bid from those of rival states.

The project was a huge financial boon for Entergy. Meta is now the largest customer in its 112-year history, and its stock price has increased over 50 percent since the project was announced in December 2024.

Local opposition has shuttered billions of dollars’ worth of data centers projects across the country. Meta’s project had no such issues with opposition — in part because the local community didn’t know about the deal until it was done.

To keep the project out of the public eye, Meta and Entergy used nondisclosure agreements with state and local officials. Even some officials who helped pass legislation to support the project didn’t know its details.

Tech companies are finding novel ways to finance the rising cost of data centers. Instead of paying for the Louisiana data center with its own money, Meta created a separate entity called Beignet LLC that would build and own the project. Blue Owl, a Wall Street investment partner, put in the bulk of the money for the joint venture. Then, Meta rented the data center from Beignet, keeping the financing off its books.

Meta gave itself the ability to exit the lease just four years after construction was finished if it no longer needed it.

The project was so large that insurance companies would not fully insure the facility if it were destroyed by a natural disaster. That scared away potential investors, but Blue Owl was still willing to take on the risk.

Richland Parish has around 20,000 residents, and many of them are optimistic about how the data center is changing the area. Construction on the project has become its own economy, employing thousands of people.

The project received tax breaks on property and equipment, so the main source of local revenue generated by the data center is sales tax. That has led to bonuses for some local teachers of as much as $50,000. Meta is also investing $1 billion in local infrastructure and $5 million into a nearby community college for job training. Once complete, the data center will employ 1,000 full-time employees.

But, as rents in the area rise to accommodate highly paid construction workers, entire trailer parks of local residents have been displaced. Some people became homeless, others moved out of the parish. Real estate developers say the project has been a trade-off, creating fortunes for some and displacing others.

After the state secured its deal with Meta, Gov. Jeff Landry codified the process with an executive order called “Louisiana Lightning Speed” to attract other projects.

The order clears the way for the state to move with similar speed and secrecy for other projects. In the case of Meta’s data center, that included allowing the Louisiana power commission to skip submitting the project to a review by an independent administrative judge to determine whether the project was in the public’s best interest. The state also did not hold any public meetings about the project until it was announced as a done deal.

Meta’s data center, from its financial engineering to the way the company secured the power supply, could become a model for other tech giants looking to build huge data centers.

The executive order is already paying off in Louisiana. In February, Amazon announced plans to build a $12 billion data center in the northwest corner of the state.

item.title: Minnesota Judge Blocks First State Ban on Prediction Markets
item.description:
A federal judge on Monday blocked a Minnesota state law that would ban prediction markets days before it was set to go into effect, siding with a federal financial regulator and two companies that had sued to stop it.

In May, Minnesota became the first state to pass a law making it a felony for most prediction markets to locally operate and advertise. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a federal agency that oversees prediction markets, and the markets Kalshi and Polymarket sued, arguing that the platforms can be regulated only at the federal level.

On Monday, Judge Kate M. Menendez of the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota granted a preliminary injunction to halt the law from going into effect on Saturday, finding that the companies faced a threat of irreparable harm. The law will remain on hold until a final ruling is made in the case.

Kalshi and Polymarket, platforms where users can place wagers on outcomes from sporting events, reality TV and more, have surged in popularity in recent months and transformed into cultural phenomena. The companies have attracted billions of dollars in trades, but their popularity has raised concerns about whether they are being manipulated by those with insider information or fueling gambling addictions.

More than a dozen states have sought to enforce anti-gambling laws already on the books to block prediction market trading. But the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued over those moves, arguing that federal regulations pre-empt state laws.

The agency has faced criticism for making what appear to be favorable decisions for prediction markets with ties to the Trump family. Donald Trump Jr. advises Kalshi and Polymarket, and he backs Polymarket financially.

President Trump has posted on Truth Social that the agency, not states, must have “exclusive authority” over prediction markets.

Some states, including New York and Washington, have won against the agency’s challenges.

But the agency has also prevailed. In April, a judge in Arizona granted a temporary restraining order to the agency to halt the state from continuing a criminal case against Kalshi.

Michael S. Selig, the agency’s chairman, said in a statement on social media on Monday night that the agency appreciated the Minnesota court’s careful consideration of the issues.

Kalshi said in court documents that as of the end of May, it had more than 90,000 users in Minnesota who were spending millions of dollars on trades.

“Today’s decision makes it clear: States cannot ban things that they don’t have jurisdiction over,” Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said in a statement.

Neal Kumar, Polymarket’s chief legal officer, said the company was looking forward to continuing to operate in Minnesota.

Minnesota lawmakers have maintained that banning prediction markets is necessary for public health and safety in a state where sports betting is illegal.

“Prediction markets are gambling, plain and simple, and Minnesota has every right to keep predatory gambling out of our communities,” Keith Ellison, Minnesota’s attorney general, said in an emailed statement. He said the state would continue to defend the law before the court.

item.title: He Helped China Repress Uyghurs. He Says He’s a Victim, Too.
item.description:
Halfway through a short speech he was giving at the German Bundestag, Zhang Yabo began to choke back tears.

Mr. Zhang had served for nine years as a police officer in Xinjiang, an enforcer in China’s campaign to surveil, detain and indoctrinate that region’s Uyghur population. At the campaign’s height, an estimated one million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities were held in internment camps.

Tens of thousands of police officers carried out China’s state oppression in Xinjiang, but Mr. Zhang is a rare voice speaking out about it. Standing before German lawmakers and human rights activists in June, he described Xinjiang as a giant prison enclosed by an “ironclad wall.” “That wall imprisoned not only countless innocent Uyghurs,” he said, “but also the souls of those ordered to enforce it.”

Mr. Zhang related the pressure of participating in China’s security apparatus: endless shifts, sleeping in the office and constant fear of punishment. After he requested asylum in Germany last summer, Chinese authorities froze his bank accounts, he said, branded him a traitor and harassed his family.

By the end of the speech, he was sobbing “like a child,” he later told me. He hurried from the room and did not return.

“All the pressure, all the fear, all the emotions that he had carried with him” seemed to break loose, said Adrian Zenz, a Xinjiang expert who attended Mr. Zhang’s speech, “like a huge dam holding back a huge amount of water.”

Mr. Zhang’s account of his time in Xinjiang corroborates what has long been documented about the Chinese Communist Party’s brutal repression of the Uyghurs while adding detail and an inside perspective to that record. It also reveals what an ordinary man pursuing upward mobility could gain, and lose, by helping to carry out those repressive policies.

Mr. Zhang provided extensive documentation of his service history, including copies of his police identification and pay and social security records, as well as photos of him at interrogations and political propaganda sessions. But I could not corroborate exactly what he did or did not do in Xinjiang; I relied on his telling of the story, and there may have been things he did not share.

The Chinese government denies committing human rights abuses in Xinjiang, describing the camps as vocational training centers created to combat terrorism and religious extremism. It says the centers were closed in 2019.

With China’s record of retaliating against citizens in exile, Mr. Zhang has shown considerable courage in coming forward as a witness to injustice. But he is asking for something more than praise; he wants to be recognized as a victim himself — a victim of the apparatus he participated in for nearly a decade.

A History of Tension For decades, the Chinese government has treated the Uyghurs, an ethnic group of about 12 million people in China’s northwestern region of Xinjiang, as a troublesome population with separatist tendencies.

Who Are the Uyghurs? The Uyghurs are a Central Asian, mostly Muslim, people, who speak their own Turkic language.

Targeting Muslims China used the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in the U.S. and Washington’s subsequent declaration of a “global war on terror” as a pretext to intensify its targeting of Uyghur Muslims.

Changing Xinjiang’s Population Chinese leaders sought to increase Xinjiang’s ethnic Han population through settlement programs, and experts estimate that tens of thousands of Uyghurs have been transferred out of the region for work.

International Condemnation The U.N. and the U.S. have condemned China’s abuses, including the use of internment camps and forced sterilization. The State Department called it genocide.

China’s Crackdown Critics of the government’s treatment of Uyghurs as well as their family members have disappeared or been detained, even abroad.

For Mr. Zhang, moving to Xinjiang, and later joining its police force, offered a way to move up in the world. Born in 1986 into a poor rural Han Chinese family, Mr. Zhang lived in a village in central Henan Province that did not have electricity until he was 8. He moved to Xinjiang for college in 2006 and stayed to teach mathematics at a rural primary school. He married a woman from his home province, and they had a son in 2011.

In late 2014, he left teaching for better pay as a guard at a detention center in the Hotan region, where about 90 percent of the population was Uyghur. His monthly wages rose to about $650, from $400 as a teacher.

For nearly two years, he said, his duties included monitoring surveillance footage, distributing food and medicine and gathering incriminating information from detainees, most of them Uyghurs. He heard screams from the interrogation rooms and saw detainees beaten up and deprived of sleep. He sometimes found broken batons when picking up the detainees. At the time, he said, he accepted the government’s claims that the men being interrogated were terrorists and separatists.

Seeking even higher pay and greater social status, Mr. Zhang took the civil service exam and formally joined the police force in late 2016 just as Beijing was about to intensify its mass detention campaign in Xinjiang. He was proud of his uniform, he said, and his monthly pay rose to about $900.

In early 2017, Chen Quanguo, the new Communist Party secretary of Xinjiang, called for a “smashing, obliterating offensive,” including, according to leaked government documents, the detention of anyone who displayed “symptoms” of religious radicalism or antigovernment views. Those symptoms could be the wearing of long beards, studying Arabic and praying.

Mr. Zhang took part in nighttime raids on Uyghur homes to confiscate Qurans and other religious items. “I was usually the first to charge in,” he recalled. “I believed they were bad people. That was what had been drilled into us at the time, that they were all bad people.”

For much of 2017, Mr. Zhang traveled in bus convoys transporting hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of Uyghur detainees to prisons across Xinjiang, which is nearly four times the size of California. The detainees were handcuffed, hooded and ordered to use plastic buckets as toilets during the journey. Mr. Zhang distributed bread and water.

“My job was serving the passengers on the bus,” he said.

In late 2018, when he was assigned to a police station, he began to grow despondent. His colleagues brought in Uyghur prisoners at all hours, he said, and he was responsible for searching them and helping determine where they would be sent. His sleep was constantly interrupted, and his superiors were short-tempered.

He was pleased to be briefly reassigned to supervise about 3,000 Uyghur laborers who had been sent to pick cotton for Han Chinese farmers. They rose at 5 a.m., traveled for hours to the cotton fields and were not returned to their dormitories until late at night.

For Mr. Zhang, it was a nice break. His main task was to make sure no one ran away or prayed.

He learned of the international criticism of forced labor in Xinjiang through statements by China’s foreign ministry and accepted the government’s claim that the accusations were false and intended to vilify China. “I didn’t think much about it,” he said. “I never paused to consider whether it was true or not.”

For years, Mr. Zhang largely accepted the orders he was given. But during the pandemic, governmental coercion began to feel personal. He said he had once been confined for about 10 days inside a village police post and, after a work trip, quarantined for nearly a month in an abandoned police station. “The pandemic was more painful because it involved me personally,” he said.

In August 2021, he was assigned to Yurushikai, a village of about 1,700 Uyghurs. About 40 percent of the adults in the village had spent time in internment camps, and some 100 were still serving time in jail, which meant that some households consisted of only children and grandparents. It was Mr. Zhang’s job, with the help of two Uyghur assistants, to investigate reports of people praying at home or missing the weekly national flag-raising ceremony or even jogging or exercising.

The government’s surveillance system generated automatic alerts for “abnormal” activity. If a household’s electricity use rose, he said, the officers would visit and ask what had kept the family awake.

Police work brought Mr. Zhang money, status and privileges: expedited treatment at hospitals, free parking. By 2023, his monthly take-home pay had risen to about $1,250.

But within the police hierarchy, he said, he was disposable. Superiors routinely insulted officers, calling them donkeys that needed to be whipped to work, Mr. Zhang said. After he missed a walkie-talkie call in December of his first year in the village, a superior punished him with 72 hours of continuous duty at a road checkpoint in freezing conditions without adequate clothing.

The overtime was relentless, and he was separated from his family for long periods. He had not celebrated Lunar New Year with his parents since 2017 and was denied leave for his sister’s wedding. On average, he could visit his wife and his son once a month.

There were also quotas to meet. Starting in 2023, he was required to produce one lead a week that could be used to justify a detention. Mr. Zhang said he had frequently failed to hit the quota and had to submit self-criticism reports and work 24-hour shifts as punishment. Working closely with the villagers began to challenge the stereotypes he had absorbed about Uyghurs. He became increasingly reluctant to enter their homes or search their private communications, even as he continued to carry out the surveillance his job required.

By September 2023, Mr. Zhang left his post.

He moved to Guangzhou in southern China to study English, hoping eventually to study abroad. He began using a VPN to get around China’s internet firewall. The first subjects he searched were “Xinjiang” and “Chen Quanguo,” the name of the region’s hard-line former party secretary. He could not believe, he said, that the facilities where he had worked, known to him as “re-education centers” and “vocational training centers,” were described online as concentration camps. Until then, he had encountered the term only in movies about World War II.

“What I found gave me terrible headaches: One side of my head said one thing, and the other said something completely different,” he said. “The conflicting accounts battled in my mind, and I couldn’t sleep at night.”

After officially resigning in early 2024, feeling wounded and in need of solace and strength, he turned to faith. He had found peace in a book about Bible stories that he had read to his son at bedtime, and in April 2025, Mr. Zhang was baptized as a Catholic in Guangzhou. Four months later, he joined a European tour with his 14-year-old son. He had already decided that if he could get away from the group, he would seek asylum.

As their tour group entered Neuschwanstein Castle, the Bavarian palace that inspired Disney’s Sleeping Beauty Castle, Mr. Zhang and his son sneaked away. They traveled to Munich and went to the headquarters of the World Uyghur Congress, an advocacy group whose name Mr. Zhang had heard many times in Xinjiang, told it was a separatist terrorist organization.

He has applied for asylum and lives in a shelter in southern Germany, where his son is staying at a foster facility not far away. Over a dinner of pasta, the 15-year-old told me that he missed Xinjiang’s spicy stir-fried rice noodles. Mr. Zhang’s wife remains in Xinjiang, and the couple have filed for divorce.

Mr. Zhang now spends his time speaking with academics, journalists and human rights groups to document how the persecution of Uyghurs was carried out.

“Of the millions of Chinese police officers, he is the only one who has come forward to speak the truth,” said Haiyuer Kuerban, an official at the World Uyghur Congress who has been helping Mr. Zhang settle in Germany. He said his organization had initially viewed Mr. Zhang with deep skepticism, but that its doubts had begun to ease after reviewing his documents.

Mr. Zenz, the Xinjiang expert who is director of China studies at the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation, a nonprofit organization in Washington, said Mr. Zhang supplied “the ground-level reality of what we had mostly inferred” from government documents, state media reports and survivor testimony.

Bjorn Alpermann, a China scholar at the University of Würzburg who has interviewed Mr. Zhang extensively, said his account offered unusually granular evidence of how repression continued after the height of the mass-internment campaign and became “routinized” in village life.

But people who have worked with Mr. Zhang in Germany told me that we knew only what he wanted us to know and that he probably knew more than he shared.

He remembers the forms he filled out, the orders he followed and the humiliations he endured in vivid detail, but is fuzzier on the worst abuses. He described hearing screams and seeing detainees after interrogations but offered fewer details about death, sexual violence and torture in detention facilities. He insisted he had been honest and forthcoming.

He also wants the world to recognize what he endured.

“My suffering was equal to, or in some respects greater than, that of the Uyghurs,” he told me repeatedly. “Why don’t you journalists write about me? Why do you only focus on the Uyghurs?”

Han Chinese officers, of course, were not forced to abandon their language or culture and, however difficult it might be, they could leave the police or Xinjiang. They were not subject to arbitrary detention, forced labor or torture. They would not be considered potential terrorists for playing basketball or doing push-ups.

“No matter how much you suffer at work, you can still go home, eat a good meal, and imagine a future,” said Mr. Kuerban, the Uyghur activist. “You do not live with the constant, paralyzing fear that something you said 10 years ago will make you disappear tomorrow.”

Still, Mr. Zhang’s experience showed how inhumanely the system treated its own operatives, Mr. Alpermann said. And for Mr. Zhang, leaving China and speaking publicly was itself a way of confronting the system.

Mr. Zhang insisted that he had never personally tortured or mistreated any Uyghurs. He described himself as a small cog in the state machinery who filled out forms, guarded facilities and handled logistics. Responsibility lay with senior officials and with the Uyghur police assistants who, he said, carried out many of the most direct and abusive tasks. Low-level Han Chinese police officers like him, he insisted, were innocent.

It is unclear whether Mr. Zhang’s self-exoneration is a form of self-protection, an inability to bear what a fuller recognition would mean or simply a habit of mind formed by years inside the system. Mr. Kuerban said he did not believe the blindness was deliberate. After repeatedly pressing Mr. Zhang, I had come to a similar conclusion: He seemed genuinely unable to see his role in the wider context of the immense injustice inflicted on the Uyghurs.

His struggle also reflected the country he came from, where the state has suppressed public memory of the Great Famine, the Cultural Revolution and the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown. Unlike Germany, where there has been decades of reckoning with Nazi complicity, China provides little space for sustained debate about complicity, guilt and responsibility.

Working inside an abusive system did not automatically make someone a monster, Mr. Kuerban said. But neither did performing a minor function, or not personally carrying out the worst abuses, eliminate responsibility.

Mr. Zhang said his faith had taught him that his responsibility now was to speak out.

“If you stay silent,” he said at the end of his Bundestag speech, “you’re part of the problem.”

item.title: Tech Stocks Tumble on Worries Over A.I. Spending and China’s Chips
item.description:
A global technology stock sell-off intensified on Tuesday, underpinned by worries over hefty bills for the build-out of artificial intelligence systems and concerns over tougher competition from China.

The Nasdaq Composite index, chock-full of big technology companies, came close on Tuesday to falling into correction, Wall Street’s term of a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent peak, before rebounding to trade flat for the day. The American chip company Micron fell over 7 percent in early trading on Tuesday, as did Advanced Micro Devices. Nvidia, the leading chipmaker, nudged lower before turning higher, but it remains more than 15 percent below its peak in May. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and A.I. company, also rebounded from an early morning slide. The stock remains more than 40 percent below its June peak.

The bumpy sell-off has taken hold over the past month, as fears about the ballooning spending by big technology companies on A.I. infrastructure and the threat of cheaper competitors undermining it have come to the fore. Cheaper A.I. models threaten the dominance of a handful of U.S.-listed companies, while competition from China has loosened South Korea’s grip on the market for memory chips critical to A.I.

On Tuesday, South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI index plunged nearly 11 percent, at one point triggering a temporary trading halt. The index has lost a third of its value over the past month but remains over 40 percent higher for the year because of the soaring rally that preceded the recent drop. Benchmark indexes in Japan and Taiwan both fell around 4 percent. Stocks in China fell over 2 percent.

The drop in South Korea spread to American exchanges. The Nasdaq 100 index, which strips out banks from the broader index making it further dependent on big tech companies, fell over 1 percent in early trading and is heading into afternoon trading almost 10 percent below its peak in June.

In Europe, the German chipmaker Infineon fell nearly 7 percent, and the Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML shed 3.5 percent. The Dow Jones industrial average, which is far less exposed to the tech industry, rose 1 percent on Tuesday, a sign that investors are homing in on concerns surrounding A.I.

The latest market tremor began on Monday, when the shares of China’s leading memory chipmaker, ChangXin Memory Technologies, began trading after a blockbuster initial public offering. The company’s stock soared nearly 500 percent on its market debut, quickly making it the most valuable company on the Shanghai exchange. It slipped 4 percent on Tuesday.

The listing prompted widespread fears that intensifying industry competition could threaten rival global memory chipmakers in South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and the United States.

Rising spending forecasts from the tech firms leading the A.I. infrastructure build out are also fanning fears. The recent market jitters intensify the spotlight on the big tech companies reporting financial results this week. Meta, Microsoft and SK Hynix, South Korea’s semiconductor giant, are set to report on Wednesday, and Apple and Amazon on Thursday.

The declines in Asia began as soon as stocks started trading on Tuesday, with A.I. and semiconductor stocks hit the hardest. Japanese flash memory maker Kioxia fell more than 18 percent. South Korean semiconductor company Samsung Electronics dropped about 13 percent.

Asian markets have been trending downward since late June, weighed down by recurring concerns over the sustainability of this year’s A.I. rally.

The staggering scale of spending required to keep up in the global A.I. race was highlighted this week with OpenAI, the parent of ChatGPT, nearing a deal to lease a $500 billion data center in Ohio, supported by $250 billion in financial backing from Nvidia. Last week, earnings reported by Tesla and Alphabet, Google’s parent company, shook the markets as they revealed their own enormous A.I. spending needs.

On Monday, the Chinese start-up Moonshot publicly released the details of its latest A.I. model, adding to investor concerns about China catching up to the United States in the A.I. arms race.

The latest market turmoil is an unwelcome turn for a region where the A.I. boom has served as a rare economic bright spot. In markets like South Korea and Taiwan, rising chip exports and soaring A.I. valuations have masked broader weakness across their domestic economies, which remain heavily dependent on energy imports from the Middle East.

The war in Iran, another major worry for investors, has rattled markets recently by restricting oil exports from the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, pushing up oil and gas prices. President Trump said on Monday that there was “a good chance” that a new round of diplomatic talks could yield a breakthrough in the monthslong war.

A recent pause in fighting has helped ease oil prices, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, falling to around $84 a barrel on Tuesday. Still, the cost of crude is up more than 15 percent since the start of the war, feeding into higher prices for gasoline and a wide range of products derived from petroleum.

item.title: A TV Judge and an R&B Singer Fought Online Trolls. They Didn’t Get Far.
item.description:
Faith Jenkins Lattimore and Kenny Lattimore had just celebrated their fifth wedding anniversary when they began hearing the rumors: She had cheated. He was secretly gay. They were battling in court.

Normally, they ignore gossip: She is a television judge, he a Grammy-nominated R&B singer; they have small children and no time for hearsay. But these stories were coming from family, friends and strangers. The couple decided to investigate.

They uncovered YouTube videos full of lies and artificially generated content regarding their marriage, a trove that was also contaminating search results about them on Google.

Plenty of people have been anonymously slimed online. Most wait for the scandal to blow over, or maybe post a rebuttal.

The Lattimores chose to fight.

They subpoenaed Google, which owns YouTube, to unmask the video creators. They sued the ones they could identify — a rare step — and spent tens of thousands of dollars and countless hours on the effort, they said.

Still, their money, legal expertise and willpower could not get all the videos removed or the lies wiped from search engine suggestions. The attention economy, the Lattimores found, is structured to reward the most eye-catching claims, allowing sensationalist but baseless narratives to spread and perpetually resurrect with little resistance from social media platforms. Their grueling, 16-month lesson in modern disinformation underscored that fighting back is not only hard — it rarely undoes the damage.

“Everybody needs to know that this is a warning — this is going to snowball if it remains unchecked,” Ms. Lattimore said.

Through a Google spokesman, YouTube said it took action against content that broke its rules and offered legal avenues for people with complaints, but otherwise did not arbitrate factual disputes.

The Lattimores, along with disinformation experts who reviewed their case, believe that the YouTube creators wanted to exploit the family’s modest fame to maximize views — and ultimately boost their payouts from YouTube by drawing more traffic to advertisements or attracting the platform’s premium subscribers.

Mr. Lattimore, 56, has been described as having a voice as “smooth and glossy as silk sheets” and has recorded 11 studio albums. Ms. Lattimore, 48, a former Miss America runner-up and assistant district attorney in Manhattan, now hosts a true-crime show on Oxygen, “Killer Relationship With Faith Jenkins.” She has also appeared as a judge on courtroom shows like “Divorce Court” and “Judge Faith.”

Each has more than 360,000 followers on Instagram — making them not stratospherically famous, but well known enough to mark them as targets. When the couple posted an anniversary video in March last year recreating a dance from their wedding, it garnered 4.4 million Facebook views and 1.4 million Instagram views.

The lurid YouTube videos soon followed. With titles like “Judge Faith CONFESSES Everything” and “Kenny Lattimore SPEAKS!” they claimed to have inside details about the couple. They were sometimes narrated in women’s voices generated by artificial intelligence, illustrated with A.I.-generated images of the spouses and captioned with fake quotes like “I couldn’t stay silent.” Altogether, the couple found 35 different YouTube videos speculating about rot in their marriage — content that Google’s A.I.-generated search overview then quoted as evidence of divorce.

None of it was true, they said.

“It was nasty,” Mr. Lattimore said in an interview near their home in Southern California. “At that point, I think I felt just completely out of control.”

The video creators may have tried to piggyback off the attention the anniversary video attracted. They may have also targeted the Lattimores because they are Black — the YouTube accounts all focused on Black celebrity culture, despite being operated almost entirely from abroad, the Lattimores said.

Black audiences have long been targeted with digital disinformation about elections, health, social justice and celebrity, said Esosa Osa, the founder of Onyx Impact, a nonprofit organization working to protect Black communities from digital harms. Black adults are also more likely than their white counterparts to regularly use social media platforms and to use hashtags.

Clickbait mercenaries “profit off of race-based tension, and they profit off of race-based engagement,” Ms. Osa said. “They’re going to go where the attention is, and Black public figures carry enormous reach and credibility and emotional resonance, so that makes them a unique target.”

José Castañeda, a spokesman for Google, said YouTube had taken down six channels in the Lattimore case and blocked the account owners from holding or creating other channels. Ten of the videos did not violate the company’s guidelines, he said; the other videos were removed by their creators.

Asked about the inaccurate divorce claim from Google’s A.I. overview, Mr. Castañeda said that when vetted information was scarce, lower-quality content might surface. He added that the overviews are updated frequently.

The Lattimores said the YouTube videos were both a personal affront and a threat to their earning potential. Family is a cornerstone of the couple’s identity online: They post glossy portraits with their toddler daughter and 2-month-old son, plug Mr. Lattimore’s album of lullabies and refer to Ms. Lattimore’s book, “Sis, Don’t Settle: How to Stay Smart in Matters of the Heart.” When the spouses promoted a South African trip for couples last winter, angry fans called them hypocrites, citing the videos’ claims that their marriage was a sham.

“This is affecting how our family members see us, how the business community sees us, whether they trust our brand,” Mr. Lattimore said.

What the couple did next was unusual, said Renee DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who studies digital influence operations and advised the Lattimores.

“When these kinds of smears happen, so many people tend to assume that they just have to deal with it,” she said. “It’s very rare to see people actually take steps and assert themselves.”

Two months after first finding the videos, Ms. Lattimore sent a formal complaint to YouTube’s legal support team, describing a “coordinated campaign of harassment, synthetic misinformation and targeted abuse.”

The videos repeatedly homed in on and misrepresented the Lattimores through false claims and A.I.-generated portrayals, violating YouTube’s rules about cyberbullying and impersonation, she wrote. They did not constitute commentary, critique or fair use, she added.

The company responded that it was “not in a position to adjudicate the veracity of postings,” according to emails shared with The New York Times. Ms. Lattimore’s only route, YouTube said, was through the court system.

So the lawyer hired a lawyer: Felton T. Newell, who has handled various entertainment disputes. He filed what’s known as a John Doe lawsuit in Los Angeles County Superior Court against the unnamed uploaders as well as Google.

To unveil the account owners, Mr. Newell subpoenaed Google. Using the company’s records, the couple identified nine YouTube account owners by name. All were men.

Willie L. Laney Jr. was the only one in the United States, according to a lawsuit the Lattimores filed against him in Maryland. His YouTube channel still peddles dramatic narratives about Black celebrities like Solange Knowles and Denzel Washington. His video titled “Judge Faith Jenkins LOSES IT!” has more than 100,000 views.

This month, a judge denied Mr. Laney’s motion to dismiss the case. Reached by email, Mr. Laney wrote that the Lattimores were painting a “skewed one-sided narrative” but did not provide details.

The Lattimores eventually dropped Google from the lawsuit. The other account owners, operating from Pakistan, India and Russia, were largely out of the couple’s reach.

The U.S. court system offers little recourse against people posting from abroad, even if they claim to be American, the couple said. Mr. Castañeda said YouTube prevents video creators from misrepresenting their locations by requiring them to verify their identity and address and only then allowing them to monetize their content.

The Lattimores did manage to pin down one foreign account owner: Shams Imran, based in Pakistan, who they said ran six channels, several of which had hundreds of thousands of followers and purported to be based in the United States. He posted (and later removed) 11 videos about the Lattimores.

Mr. Imran fought to prevent Google from identifying him, but the Lattimores prevailed and reached a $5,000 settlement in August. Mr. Imran and his lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.

More than a year after their ordeal began, the Lattimores have gotten further in their defensive campaign than most — which is still not very far. Several videos remain visible. Some of the YouTube operators changed their account names and kept posting. “Divorce” is still one of the first suggestions when users search for the couple on Google. Interest in the spouses spilled over onto platforms such as X, where the number of posts mentioning them has surged over the past year, according to Peakmetrics, an analytics company.

“I can’t advise people to go down the rabbit hole of litigation — it’s just not a sustainable response to dealing with this online defamation,” said Ms. Lattimore, who throughout the fight was also struggling with a difficult pregnancy. “That’s why YouTube has to do something — it’s really their responsibility at this point.”

The couple are now pushing the platform to make broader changes.

In February, they appeared with Ben Crump, a civil rights lawyer, at a news conference announcing the complaints he had filed with the U.S. attorney general and the Federal Trade Commission about YouTube’s monetization policies. The couple will also lobby Congress this summer, joining a bipartisan group that has long sought to change Section 230, a federal law that shields internet companies from liability over the content they host.

“You think it’s going to stop with just us, as public figures?” Ms. Lattimore said. “It’s a very low bar to entry into this kind of business.”
